source: Citywide milestones from NYC DOT and the Mayor's Office; CB6 entries from the board's own votes. Daylighting status as of the plan's release on September 15, 2026.

items.t: CB6 backs a Neighborhood Slow Zone for Boerum Hill
items.x: Before Vision Zero existed, the board voted to slow a whole neighborhood to 20 mph rather than fix one crossing at a time. DOT's own evaluation later found the 85th percentile speed dropped from about 25 mph to just over 20.
items.ahead: Fourteen months before the city adopted Vision Zero

items.t: New York City adopts Vision Zero, under a Park Slope mayor
items.x: Mayor Bill de Blasio, a Park Slope resident of this district, launches the first Vision Zero program in the United States: a multi-agency commitment to eliminate traffic deaths and serious injuries, built on the idea that people make mistakes and a street should not make a mistake fatal.

items.t: CB6 votes for the state bill cutting the speed limit to 25 mph
items.x: 33 to nothing, five months before the law took effect. Board members argued the district had seen too many tragedies and that drivers had to slow down.
items.ahead: Five months before the 25 mph limit took effect

items.t: The citywide default speed limit drops to 25 mph
items.x: Unless a street is signed otherwise, 25 mph becomes the law in New York City.

items.t: CB6 writes to the Mayor and DOT demanding safety work on 9th Street
items.x: A full-corridor request, unanimous, years before the protected bike lane and the leading pedestrian intervals arrived.

items.t: CB6 votes to get Van Brunt Street off the truck route network
items.x: Backing Resilient Red Hook, 33 to 5. DOT published its first truck route network overhaul six years later, effective October 2026.
items.ahead: Six years before DOT redrew the truck route network

items.t: Speed cameras go 24/7
items.x: Albany lets the city run its school zone speed cameras around the clock. Most deaths happen outside school hours.

items.t: CB6 votes for the city to obey the state 20-foot rule at intersections
items.x: New York State bans parking within 20 feet of a crosswalk. New York City exempts itself. The board voted to end the exemption. Daylighting.
items.ahead: A year before the universal daylighting bill was introduced at the Council

items.t: Sammy's Law passes in Albany
items.x: Named for Sammy Cohen Eckstein, killed by a driver on Prospect Park West in 2013, the law finally lets New York City set speed limits below 25 mph.

items.t: Universal daylighting lands at the City Council as Intro 1138
items.x: Council Member Julie Won's bill would ban parking within 20 feet of every intersection and require DOT to harden 1,000 corners a year. It reached 27 co-sponsors.

items.t: Congestion pricing begins
items.x: Tolling below 60th Street in Manhattan. In its first year the MTA reported 11 percent fewer vehicles entering the zone and higher bus and subway ridership.

items.t: CB6 calls for hardened daylighting at every intersection in the city
items.x: After a presentation on daylighting, the committee voted for three things: the city opts back in to the state 20-foot rule, physical barriers at every intersection, and support for the Council daylighting bill. Passed unanimously.
items.ahead: Seven months before the Council let the bill die

items.t: CB6 backs the Court Street redesign, with conditions that read like this plan
items.x: Concrete curbs instead of plastic, hardened daylighting on the side streets, 15 to 20 mph under Sammy's Law, leading pedestrian intervals at every crossing, longer loading zone hours. Fifteen months before the Mayor's plan named the same tools.
items.ahead: Fifteen months before the plan made these citywide commitments

items.t: CB6 calls for an end to criminal summonses for delivery cyclists
items.x: And for the city to make app companies classify delivery workers as employees with legal equipment. The 2026 plan devotes a goal to regulating third-party delivery platforms.
items.ahead: Fifteen months before the plan took up delivery platform accountability

items.t: The Council lets the daylighting bill die
items.x: The Speaker pulls Intro 1138 from the final stated meeting of the session. Twenty-seven co-sponsors and it never gets a vote. It has to start over in the new session.

items.t: CB6 votes for a district-wide 20 mph slow zone
items.x: Under Sammy's Law, on every street with no more than two lanes in one direction, with signal retiming and camera enforcement, and a call for 20 mph citywide. Unanimous.
items.ahead: Six months before the plan committed to 20 mph neighborhood zones

items.t: The city commits to 15 mph School Slow Zones at every eligible school
items.x: As many as 2,300 sites serving 3,200 schools, with speed camera enforcement.

items.t: CB6 votes to move parking enforcement from the NYPD back to DOT
items.x: Where it sat before 1996, so it gets the attention it needs and the NYPD can focus on crime. Manhattan Community Board 6 passed a version of ours. It is not in the Mayor's plan.
items.ahead: Still not in the city's plan

items.t: CB6 approves the Hamilton Avenue changes, with HAWK signals
items.x: New crosswalks, lane reductions and delineators to stop illegal right turns, with the street direction changes sent back for more community input.

items.t: Vision Zero Reimagined
items.x: Eight goals, eleven marquee actions, 111 actions across 19 agencies. It commits to hardened daylighting or better at a minimum of 1,000 intersections a year. It does not end the city's exemption from the state 20-foot rule, and it does not commit to daylighting every intersection.
